titleStmt.title: Monkeys show recognition without priming in a classification task
titleStmt.author: Basile
Hampton

bibl.title: Monkeys show recognition without priming in a classification task

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: null-result
span.quote: Across 11 experiments, monkeys did not show priming, nor did they show any reliable benefit of having seen to-be-classified images.

span.label: perceptual (repetition) priming in monkeys
span.quote: We tested for priming in rhesus monkeys using procedures similar to those that have been effective in humans.

span.label: behavioural-experiment
span.quote: We tested six adult male rhesus monkeys ( Macaca mulatta ; mean age at start of testing = 3.2 years).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: The visual processing that supports recognition is encapsulated from the processing that supports classification, so remembering an image cannot feed forward to help classify a degraded version of it.
span.quote: This suggests that the visual processing necessary for recognition is cognitively encapsulated from that necessary for classification.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Pigeons and monkeys classify by different routes — local features versus global shape — which is offered as the explanation for why priming appeared in pigeons but not here.
span.quote: Thus, it appears that unlike our monkeys, pigeons are more likely to process local rather than global features in classifications tasks.

span.label: The study may simply have failed to identify the conditions under which priming would appear in monkeys.
span.quote: Third, priming could be a type of memory shared among humans, monkeys, and pigeons, but the current study was not designed appropriately to detect it.

span.label: Despite exploring many manipulations, the critical conditions for producing a memory effect on classification may have been missed.
span.quote: Although we based our methods on studies that have showed positive evidence of priming in humans and pigeons, and we explored a large number of reasonable manipulations, it is possible we failed to identify the critical conditions under which we would find priming, or indeed any memory effect on classification, in monkeys.

span.label: The one significant priming effect obtained (Experiment 5, blur mask) is treated by the authors as unreliable and possibly a Type I error.
span.quote: Although the accuracy benefit seen with primed images was statistically significant, it should be interpreted with caution.

span.label: the human occluded-picture-naming priming paradigm is converted into a classification task so it can be run on monkeys
span.quote: As in priming studies in which humans were asked to name partially occluded images that they either had or had not seen previously ( Mitchell, 2006 ; Snodgrass & Feenan, 1990 ), we required monkeys to classify partially occluded photographs that they either had or had not seen previously.

span.label: perceptual priming
span.quote: Humans show visual perceptual priming by identifying degraded images faster and more accurately if they have seen the original images, while simultaneously failing to recognize the same images

span.label: priming
span.quote: Thus, priming is cognitively distinct from explicit memory, long-lasting, early developing, and depends on neural systems distinct from those serving explicit memory. Because priming is automatic, effortless, unconscious, and neuroanatomically separate from sophisticated forms of memory such as episodic memory, researchers have theorized that it may be evolutionary old

span.label: explicit memory
span.quote: Thus, priming is cognitively distinct from explicit memory, long-lasting, early developing, and depends on neural systems distinct from those serving explicit memory. Because priming is automatic, effortless, unconscious, and neuroanatomically separate from sophisticated forms of memory such as episodic memory, researchers have theorized that it may be evolutionary old

span.label: recognition
span.quote: Experiment 10 showed that monkeys remembered the primes sufficiently to recognize them while simultaneously showing no facilitation of classification. This suggests that the visual processing necessary for recognition is cognitively encapsulated from that necessary for classification

span.label: classification
span.quote: Experiment 10 showed that monkeys remembered the primes sufficiently to recognize them while simultaneously showing no facilitation of classification. This suggests that the visual processing necessary for recognition is cognitively encapsulated from that necessary for classification

span.label: repetition suppression
span.quote: a neural mechanism theorized to underlie priming, repetition suppression ( Wiggs & Martin, 1998 ), has been observed in electrophysiological recordings in nonhuman primates ( Mcmahon & Olson, 2007 ). This theory and evidence leads us to expect priming in monkeys

span.label: search image
span.quote: The phenomenon of perceptual priming is also similar to, but distinct from, the concept of “specific searching image” in studies of insect predation by birds ( Tinbergen, 1960 ). After repeated exposure to cryptic prey, such as when foraging for camouflaged moths, birds may form a mental image that facilitates subsequent searches for that prey. However, unlike the facilitation caused by perceptual priming, the facilitation caused by forming a search image is short lived ( Langley, Riley, Bond, & Goel, 1996 ) and diminished by divided attention ( Dukas & Kamil, 2001 ). This suggests that formation of a search image acts as a type of short-term attentional priming ( Blough, 2001 ; Reid & Shettleworth, 1992 ; Shettleworth, 2010 ) rather than the long-term perceptual priming seen in humans

span.label: priming as IMPLICIT - named by the paper as the critical feature of the theories it is testing, and stated as a double requirement: subjects identify primed material better AND cannot explicitly remember it. The effect is defined partly by a FAILURE that has to accompany it, which is why a study finding memory for the primes is testing something the definition cares about
span.quote: A critical feature of theories of the organization of human memory is that priming is implicit. Subjects are better at identifying primed material even when they cannot explicitly remember

span.label: priming defined by a PROPERTY LIST rather than by a mechanism - automatic, effortless, unconscious, neuroanatomically separate from sophisticated forms of memory such as episodic memory. Every item is a contrast with something else, and it is precisely this shape of definition that licenses the leap to evolutionary age: a capacity that needs none of the expensive machinery is assumed to have come first
span.quote: Because priming is automatic, effortless, unconscious, and neuroanatomically separate from sophisticated forms of memory such as episodic memory, researchers have theorized that it may be evolutionary old

span.label: the PHYLOGENETIC ASSUMPTION, named as an assumption in the abstract: priming is `commonly thought, WITH LITTLE EVIDENCE, to be widely distributed phylogenetically`. The paper's target is not a finding but a belief its field holds without having tested it - and the only prior nonhuman evidence it can find is one study in pigeons
span.quote: Such priming is commonly thought, with little evidence, to be widely distributed phylogenetically. Following Brodbeck (1997) , we trained rhesus monkeys

span.label: search image versus perceptual priming - a neighbouring concept separated by two stated measurements rather than by definition: the search image is SHORT LIVED and is DIMINISHED BY DIVIDED ATTENTION, so it is classed as short-term ATTENTIONAL priming rather than the long-term PERCEPTUAL priming seen in humans. Two literatures using one word, told apart by duration and by whether attention matters
span.quote: The phenomenon of perceptual priming is also similar to, but distinct from, the concept of “specific searching image” in studies of insect predation by birds ( Tinbergen, 1960 ). After repeated exposure to cryptic prey, such as when foraging for camouflaged moths, birds may form a mental image that facilitates subsequent searches for that prey. However, unlike the facilitation caused by perceptual priming, the facilitation caused by forming a search image is short lived ( Langley, Riley, Bond, & Goel, 1996 ) and diminished by divided attention ( Dukas & Kamil, 2001 ). This suggests that formation of a search image acts as a type of short-term attentional priming ( Blough, 2001 ; Reid & Shettleworth, 1992 ; Shettleworth, 2010 ) rather than the long-term perceptual priming seen in humans

span.label: `priming` and `perceptual priming` are used at DIFFERENT GRAIN in different parts of the argument, and the split is systematic rather than casual: where the paper reasons about memory SYSTEMS - dissociation from explicit memory, survival in amnesia, evolutionary age - it writes bare `priming`; where it describes the visual effect it measures, and where it fences that effect off from the search image, it writes `perceptual priming`. The general term carries the theory and the specific term carries the experiment
span.quote: Thus, priming is cognitively distinct from explicit memory, long-lasting, early developing, and depends on neural systems distinct from those serving explicit memory. Because priming is automatic, effortless, unconscious, and neuroanatomically separate from sophisticated forms of memory such as episodic memory, researchers have theorized that it may be evolutionary old

span.label: a null defended rather than reported - the paper argues its own absence of evidence is not absence of power, on three separate grounds: priming is routinely seen in SINGLE human subjects, the pigeon result that motivated the study used FEWER subjects than this one, and the same animals demonstrably remembered the primes. The last is the one that matters, because it rules out the animals not having encoded the images at all
span.quote: Our null results are unlikely to be the product of low statistical power. First, it is unlikely that the size of our subject pool masked detection of priming. Priming is often seen in case studies of single human subjects ( Gabrieli et al., 1990 ; Hamann & Squire, 1997 ), and the positive evidence from pigeons comes from a study using fewer subjects than the current experiment ( Brodbeck, 1997 ). Second, it is unlikely that our measures were overly-noisy or that there were insufficient opportunities to observe priming. Each experiment used a large number of trials, which reduced measurement noise for each subject, and we conducted a large number of experiments, which provided many opportunities to observe priming. Third, our methods were sufficient to detect memory for the primes

span.label: builds-on → Brodbeck (1997)
span.quote: Following Brodbeck (1997) , we trained rhesus monkeys ( Macaca mulatta ) to categorize photographs according to content (e.g., birds, fish, flowers, people).

span.label: contradicts → Brodbeck (1997)
span.quote: We failed to replicate the findings of the single study of priming in nonhumans ( Brodbeck, 1997 ).

span.label: contradicts → Mcmahon & Olson (2007)
span.quote: Given the short delays used (mean = 1.9 seconds), it is likely the monkeys would have recognized the primes and, thus, this study does not provide evidence for implicit priming in monkeys.

span.label: perceptual priming —distinct-from→ search image
span.note: differs in: DURATION AND ATTENTIONAL DEPENDENCE - the search image is short lived and is diminished by divided attention, which is why the paper files it as short-term attentional priming rather than long-term perceptual priming · strength of the relation: 0.9 — The paper's own phrase is `similar to, but distinct from`, and it does not leave the distinction as an assertion: both differentiating properties are cited to experiments. This is the shape the corpus wants - a boundary drawn with measurements.
span.quote: The phenomenon of perceptual priming is also similar to, but distinct from, the concept of “specific searching image” in studies of insect predation by birds ( Tinbergen, 1960 ). After repeated exposure to cryptic prey, such as when foraging for camouflaged moths, birds may form a mental image that facilitates subsequent searches for that prey. However, unlike the facilitation caused by perceptual priming, the facilitation caused by forming a search image is short lived ( Langley, Riley, Bond, & Goel, 1996 ) and diminished by divided attention ( Dukas & Kamil, 2001 ). This suggests that formation of a search image acts as a type of short-term attentional priming ( Blough, 2001 ; Reid & Shettleworth, 1992 ; Shettleworth, 2010 ) rather than the long-term perceptual priming seen in humans

span.label: priming —distinct-from→ explicit memory
span.note: differs in: WHETHER IT SURVIVES AMNESIA AND WHICH NEURAL SYSTEM CARRIES IT - the separation is the definition rather than a finding about it, which is what makes this record's null result awkward for the theory · strength of the relation: 0.9 — Recorded because the dissociation is doing definitional work: priming is IDENTIFIED by being separable from explicit memory. A monkey that recognises the primes but shows no priming is a dissociation running the other way.
span.quote: Thus, priming is cognitively distinct from explicit memory, long-lasting, early developing, and depends on neural systems distinct from those serving explicit memory. Because priming is automatic, effortless, unconscious, and neuroanatomically separate from sophisticated forms of memory such as episodic memory, researchers have theorized that it may be evolutionary old

span.label: repetition suppression —causes→ priming
span.note: direction on the measure: increases · strength of the relation: 0.7 — Weight 0.7 - the LOWEST on this record, and deliberately. The paper reports this as a theorised mechanism it is about to find fault with: the neural signature is present in monkeys and the behavioural effect is not. Recorded as the literature's claim, not as this paper's.
span.quote: a neural mechanism theorized to underlie priming, repetition suppression ( Wiggs & Martin, 1998 ), has been observed in electrophysiological recordings in nonhuman primates ( Mcmahon & Olson, 2007 ). This theory and evidence leads us to expect priming in monkeys

span.label: recognition —distinct-from→ classification
span.note: differs in: WHETHER MEMORY FOR AN IMAGE REACHES THE PROCESS AT ALL - the same remembered image supports recognition and does nothing for classification, which the paper reads as cognitive encapsulation between the two · strength of the relation: 0.85 — THE RESULT, stated as a relation between two tasks rather than as an effect size. The paper's last word on it is `presents a puzzle`, and the weight says so.
span.quote: Experiment 10 showed that monkeys remembered the primes sufficiently to recognize them while simultaneously showing no facilitation of classification. This suggests that the visual processing necessary for recognition is cognitively encapsulated from that necessary for classification

span.label: t-test
span.quote: Paired t-tests were used to compare performance on primed trials to that on unprimed trials, and one-sample t-tests were used to compare performance to chance levels.

span.label: arcsine transformation
span.quote: All proportions were arcsine transformed prior to statistical analysis to better approximate normality ( Aron & Aron, 1999 ).

span.label: significance level (alpha), two-tailed testing
span.quote: All statistical tests were two-tailed with α = .05.

span.label: effect size (Cohen's d)
span.quote: Monkeys were significantly more accurate at classifying primed images than unprimed images ( Figure 7 , left; t (5) = 4.4, p < .01, d = 1.8).

span.label: p-value
span.quote: Monkeys were not more accurate at classifying primed images than unprimed images ( Figure 3 , left; t (5) = 0.6, p = .6).

span.label: median
span.quote: Latency was the median time from onset of the sample to selection of one of the symbols on correct trials only.

span.label: Type I error
span.quote: These results fail to replicate the memory effect observed in Experiment 5 under conditions in which the effect should have been strengthened, suggesting that the effect seen in Experiment 5 was a Type I error.

span.label: Across eleven experiments rhesus monkeys showed no priming: previously seen images conferred no reliable advantage when degraded versions had to be classified.
span.quote: Across 11 experiments, monkeys did not show priming, nor did they show any reliable benefit of having seen to-be-classified images.

span.label: The same monkeys did recognise the prime images, both masked and unmasked, at the same memory interval at which no priming appeared.
span.quote: In contrast, monkeys did recognize the primed images significantly above chance both when unmasked and when masked ( Figure 12 , right; unmasked: t (5) = 4.7, p < .01, d = 1.9; masked: t (5) = 4.4, p < .01, d = 1.8).

span.label: The single significant priming result (the blur-mask experiment) failed to replicate under stronger conditions and is interpreted as a Type I error.
span.quote: These results fail to replicate the memory effect observed in Experiment 5 under conditions in which the effect should have been strengthened, suggesting that the effect seen in Experiment 5 was a Type I error.

span.label: Shuffling the visible fragments of a masked image lowered classification accuracy, showing the monkeys used global arrangement rather than isolated local features.
span.quote: Scrambling the masked images significantly decreased classification accuracy compared to intact masked images ( Figure 11 ; t (5) = 5.2, p < .01, d = 2.1).

span.label: The classification was based on global form, exactly the kind of process that memory for the intact image should have facilitated.
span.quote: Together, these results indicate that the monkeys classified images based on global form, a process that would be expected to be facilitated by memory of the image.

span.label: A close methodological replication of the only positive nonhuman priming study (in pigeons) produced no priming in monkeys.
span.quote: Under conditions similar to those in which pigeons showed a memory effect of having recently seen the to-be-classified stimuli ( Brodbeck, 1997 ), monkeys did not.

span.label: The combination of intact recognition with absent facilitation constitutes a dissociation between remembering an image and classifying it.
span.quote: Experiment 10 showed that monkeys remembered the primes sufficiently to recognize them while simultaneously showing no facilitation of classification.

span.label: perceptual priming (repetition priming)
span.quote: In the lab, this phenomenon is explored in studies of perceptual priming (sometimes called repetition priming; hereafter, priming; Tulving & Schacter, 1990 ).

span.label: specific searching image
span.quote: After repeated exposure to cryptic prey, such as when foraging for camouflaged moths, birds may form a mental image that facilitates subsequent searches for that prey.

span.label: perceptual closure
span.quote: Priming in humans is thought to rely on the shape of the primed image and on perceptual closure, our tendency to mentally fill-in occluded areas of an image ( Snodgrass & Feenan, 1990 ; Wiggs & Martin, 1998 ); therefore, monkeys may not show priming if they classify images based on hyper-local cues.

span.label: accuracy (operational definition)
span.quote: For all experiments, accuracy was measured as the proportion of images correctly classified.

span.label: latency (operational definition)
span.quote: Latency was the median time from onset of the sample to selection of one of the symbols on correct trials only.

span.label: prime status of the test image (primed vs. unprimed/novel)
span.term: prime status of the test image (primed vs. unprimed/novel)
span.quote: Of the four masked images in each block of eight trials, two were familiar, one was a primed image from the initial 12 trials at the start of the session, and one was an unprimed image that was completely novel.

span.label: classification accuracy
span.quote: For all experiments, accuracy was measured as the proportion of images correctly classified.

span.label: classification latency
span.quote: Latency was the median time from onset of the sample to selection of one of the symbols on correct trials only.

span.label: type of image degradation (checkerboard mask vs. blur mask)
span.term: type of image degradation (checkerboard mask vs. blur mask)
span.quote: Procedures were the same as in Experiment 5 with the exception that the checkerboard mask was changed to a blur mask.

span.label: image quality (color, grayscale, line drawings)
span.quote: This finding was robust across manipulations of image quality (color, grayscale, line drawings), type of image degradation (occlusion, blurring), levels of processing, and number of repetitions of the prime.

span.label: category control images preceding unprimed trials
span.term: category control images preceding unprimed trials
span.quote: These category control images controlled for any effect of increased attention or motivation caused by having the primed trial preceded by an image of the same category.

span.label: six — number of adult male rhesus monkeys tested throughout the study
span.quote: We tested six adult male rhesus monkeys ( Macaca mulatta ; mean age at start of testing = 3.2 years).

span.label: 288 / 288 — primed and unprimed trials collected per monkey in Experiment 1
span.quote: We ran twenty-four sessions, resulting in 288 primed trials and 288 unprimed trials for each monkey.

span.label: 3.1% — the absolute accuracy advantage for primed images in the one experiment that reached significance, later attributed to Type I error
span.quote: It represents a relatively small absolute improvement (3.1%), and was the lone significant result of our study thus far.

span.label: 80% / 81% — the occlusion level required in the pigeon-replication and the accuracy it produced
span.quote: Monkeys required the highest mask level, which occluded 80% of the image and brought performance down to 81% during phase 3.

span.label: 98% — the monkeys' accuracy on the cats-versus-cars discrimination by the final training session
span.quote: Monkeys learned the cats/cars discrimination to over 80% accuracy by the end of the first training session and 98% accuracy by the final training session.

span.label: t (5) = 0.6, p = .6 — the null test of primed versus unprimed classification accuracy in Experiment 1, typical of the paper's null results
span.quote: Monkeys were not more accurate at classifying primed images than unprimed images ( Figure 3 , left; t (5) = 0.6, p = .6).

span.label: d = 1.9 — effect size for recognition of unmasked primes, the effect that was present while priming was absent
span.quote: In contrast, monkeys did recognize the primed images significantly above chance both when unmasked and when masked ( Figure 12 , right; unmasked: t (5) = 4.7, p < .01, d = 1.9; masked: t (5) = 4.4, p < .01, d = 1.8).
